source.title: STAIR: Improving Safety Alignment with Introspective Reasoning
source.authors: Yi-Chi Zhang; Si-Yuan Zhang; Yao Huang; Ze-Yu Xia; Zheng-Wei Fang; Xiao Yang; Ran-Jie Duan; Dong Yan; Yin-Peng Dong; Jun Zhu

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether safety-aware reasoning training and inference-time search improve safety under harmful prompts and jailbreaks, using behavioral benchmarks rather than the original studies’ methods.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates harmful-query refusal and jailbreak robustness after its own reasoning-based safety training, and reports qualitative cases where a jailbreak begins with a compliant opening. It does not test few-example harmful or benign fine-tuning as a cause of safety loss, per-token KL, or safety localization in weights. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper takes 'shallow alignment' (Qi et al.) as motivation (Fig. 1, Intro). It then reports only how its own reasoning-based safety training (STAIR) compares with other alignment methods on StrongReject (PAIR/PAP jailbreaks), XsTest and similar refusal benchmarks. It does not: (a) fine-tune a safety-trained model on harmful or benign data to see whether safety is lost; (b) measure per-token KL or anything by response position; (c) isolate prefilling, suffixes or decoding changes; (d) localize safety in weights; (e) test whether data or objective causes shallowness; or (f) measure whether STAIR spreads safety beyond the first response tokens. PAIR and PAP are semantic, role-play jailbreaks, not opening-bypass attacks. XsTest-unsafe is plain harmful prompts. The benchmark rows therefore compare the study's method against baselines and do not measure what any version names.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that structured safety-aware reasoning, iterative self-improvement with SI-MCTS and step-level DPO, and PRM-guided test-time search improve safety and jailbreak resistance while preserving or improving general capability. With test-time scaling, STAIR reaches Claude-3.5-level StrongReject goodness (about 0.94). They argue direct-refusal ('System 1', shallow) alignment is why jailbreaks succeed, but do not test that claim.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains structured chain-of-thought responses, performs iterative safety-informed MCTS and step-level DPO, and uses a process reward model for optional inference-time search. It does not reproduce the original fine-tuning, KL-position, or weight-localization methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by model, training stage, benchmark, and inference search method. The LLaMA STAIR-SFT XsTest refusal rate is below its base rate, while later stages rise; test-time search changes StrongReject scores.

fits_no_version.finding: Reasoning-based safety training (STAIR) raises StrongReject PAIR/PAP goodness from 0.4054 to 0.8798 (LLaMA-3.1-8B) and from 0.3808 to 0.8486 (Qwen-2-7B), above SFT, DPO, SACPO and Self-Rewarding baselines (Table 1). With test-time beam search, LLaMA reaches 0.9391 (Table 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training models to reason about risk before refusing improves robustness to semantic jailbreaks relative to direct-refusal alignment.

fits_no_version.finding: In three qualitative PAIR cases, a DPO-aligned baseline refuses the plain harmful prompt. It complies once the prompt adds role-play and requests the opening 'Sure, I'm happy to help'. STAIR-DPO-3 refuses all three.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Direct-refusal aligned models comply with disguised jailbreaks that request a compliant opening (qualitative; not separable from disguise).

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The excerpt reports no uncertainty estimates for the benchmark results. The safety reward is partly self-rated by the trained model, with a rule-based refusal check used in some cases. The appendix jailbreak evidence consists of three qualitative examples, not a measured success rate. StrongReject is reported as an average over two jailbreak methods in the main table.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 WildChat and Stereotype metrics are omitted; the selected rows prioritize StrongReject jailbreak robustness and XsTest harmful-query refusal, and the 60-row limit does not require their inclusion once these versions are covered. Other auxiliary comparisons in Tables 6–7 and additional test-time scaling figure results were not extracted.

untested.parts: No harmful fine-tuning of a safety-trained model.
No benign-only fine-tuning measured for safety loss.
No per-token KL or position-wise measure.

No prefilling, adversarial suffix or decoding-change attack. PAIR/PAP are semantic jailbreaks. Appendix cases only include an in-prompt request for a compliant opening, confounded with role-play, with no rate.
Asserts that direct-refusal training causes shallow alignment, but tests no data or objective as cause.
STAIR is reasoning-before-refusal training. The paper never measures whether safety is spread beyond the first response tokens, and never tests prefill or fine-tuning attacks against it.

missing.what: Per-attack StrongReject breakdown (None / PAIR / PAP-Mis) for STAIR-DPO-3 (1.0000 / 0.7919 / 0.9677), for o1-like models, and for Deliberative Alignment reproductions.
missing.versions: none (relevant to V7 only if a reviewer treats STAIR as a deepening fix)

missing.what: Commercial-model StrongReject per attack, and the STAIR beam-search average of 0.9391.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked every benchmark row to V4 and V7. Those rows are the study's own method compared with baselines on semantic-jailbreak and plain-harmful benchmarks. None of them measures response-position depth, prefilling or fine-tuning attacks, so all are relinked to none and no verdicts are given. Shallow alignment is cited only as motivation. Self-rated safety rewards and the absence of uncertainty estimates are further limits.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test harmful fine-tuning as an intervention that removes refusal.
Does not isolate ordinary or benign-only fine-tuning and measure its effect on harmful compliance.
No per-token KL or other response-position measurement.
Qualitative jailbreak examples include an instructed compliant opening, but the paper does not isolate prefilling as an intervention or test decoding changes.
No weight or rank localization test.
The paper discusses direct-refusal alignment as a possible reason for jailbreak vulnerability, but does not test the data or objective as the cause of shallow alignment.

Tests its structured-reasoning training and test-time search on safety benchmarks, but does not directly measure whether safety is spread across response positions or whether the effect persists beyond the reported benchmarks.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Baseline DPO model on the three illustrative jailbreak prompts with compliant openings
reader_labels.reason: The baseline is described as complying with the harmful requests in all three examples (R37, R39, R41). These are qualitative cases, not a measured rate.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: STAIR-DPO-3 on the three illustrative jailbreak prompts with compliant openings
reader_labels.reason: STAIR-DPO-3 refuses in the paired examples rather than being bypassed by the requested opening (R38, R40, R42); this limits generalization from the baseline examples.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: STAIR training stages on StrongReject jailbreak prompts and XsTest harmful prompts
reader_labels.reason: Across both model families, later STAIR stages report higher StrongReject goodness and XsTest refusal rates than the corresponding base models (R11–R18, R29–R36).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The refusal rate at the initial STAIR-SFT stage is below the base-model rate, before increasing in later iterations (R2, R12, R14, R16, R18).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Best-of-4 inference on StrongReject for STAIR-SFT and STAIR-DPO-1
reader_labels.reason: Both self-rewarding and PRM-based Best-of-4 inference raise the StrongReject goodness score over regular inference, though the increases are modest (R43–R46).
